To help you to properly observe the laws laid out in this chapter it is necessary to record, on
an ongoing basis, the arrival and cessation dates of the menstrual cycle. Many poskim require
this to be done in written form. Beyond this, experience has consistently shown that the only
way to accurately observe this concept is to write it down. This is simple and not time-
Even if the couple is unclear about all the details of how to calculate these dates, it is still
important to record the onset and cessation dates, as will be explained further. The reason is
that their Rabbi, mentor, or confidant will have a much simpler job of helping them organize
their personal records if these dates are presented in an orderly fashion.
Although many women have an intuitive awareness of when to expect their menstruation,
it is not on this intuition that the couple is to base their actions, rather they must record and
project these dates according to the directives of our sages, as will be explained in this chapter.
And you shall caution the Jews to guard against their impurity.
Based on the above verse, the Talmudic sages, of blessed memory, established a requirement
that the husband and wife separate on the date(s) when the next menstrual period can be
. This legislation was intended to prevent any opportunity for conjugal
intimacy at the time of the anticipated appearance of menstruation.

Long cycles erase shorter non-established previous cycles. For example: in our
previous illustration of the Interval Cycle, we recorded a cycle of 46 half day
periods. If the next cycle were 47 half day periods or longer, it would erase and
displace the need to consider the old cycle of 46.
On the other hand, shorter cycles do not erase longer non-established previous
cycles. In the previous example, if the next cycle was 45 half day periods [or
shorter], then the following month they would separate both on the 45
